marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q007.takeaway: Sensory-stimulus intensity is encoded by afferent firing frequency and recruitment of additional receptors.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q007.displayText:
The source-keyed statement is that the frequency of action potentials in an afferent fiber reflects the intensity of its receptor's stimulus. Intensity is also encoded by recruiting a larger number of sensory receptors, so firing frequency and population recruitment work together.

This differs from the Weber–Fechner relationship: perceived magnitude varies with the logarithm of stimulus intensity, not in direct proportion to intensity itself.

A maintained touch does not produce a constant discharge from every receptor. Adaptation reduces firing during a sustained stimulus, which is why clothing does not continue to evoke an unnecessary constant stream of touch signals. The source table below preserves its distinction between slowly adapting (tonic) receptors and rapidly adapting (phasic) receptors.
emphasis: recruiting a larger number of sensory receptors

displayTables.title: Sensory receptor adaptation
rows: Merkel discs, Ruffini endings, joint-capsule receptors, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs
Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner corpuscles, and hair-end organs

rationales.a: Weber–Fechner relates perceived magnitude to the logarithm of stimulus intensity, rather than direct proportionality to intensity.
rationales.b: A touch receptor adapts during sustained stimulation, so its afferent discharge does not remain constant.
rationales.c: Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting; several other listed receptors, including Merkel and Ruffini endings, adapt slowly.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q008.takeaway: Aδ fibers carry fast, relatively well-localized first pain; C fibers carry slow, diffuse pain, so Aδ fibers do not transmit slow pain.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q008.displayText:
Aδ fibers are thinly myelinated and conduct the fast, sharp first pain that is also called epicritic pain. Their central terminals release glutamate, and their signals travel mainly through the neospinothalamic pathway.

C fibers are unmyelinated, polymodal nociceptors that conduct the slower, diffuse or burning component (protopathic pain) through paleospinothalamic pathways. The source compares their slower conduction and substance P with the faster Aδ component and glutamate. It also notes that neuropathic pain may be burning, dull, and poorly localized; those descriptors can overlap with slow pain but do not make all neuropathic pain a C-fiber mechanism.

Thus Aδ fibers transmit fast/first/epicritic pain, not slow pain. The source comparison below preserves the listed stimuli, fiber properties, tracts, velocities, and pain components. Transmitter associations are retained in the prose above; nociceptor signaling can involve more than one transmitter and pathway.

rationales.b: Epicritic pain is the fast, discriminative pain associated with Aδ transmission, so Aδ fibers do transmit it.
rationales.c: Fast pain is the characteristic Aδ-mediated component, making this the opposite of the statement asked for.
rationales.d: First pain is the rapid, sharp Aδ-mediated component; slow second pain is predominantly carried by C fibers.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q009.takeaway: Bradykinin is the source-keyed answer among these algogens, but the source itself flags the claim that it is universally the “most potent” as controversial.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q009.displayText:
The source-keyed answer is bradykinin. It is an endogenous algogen released in tissue injury and can directly excite nociceptors. Other listed or source-named algogenic mediators include serotonin, histamine, potassium ions, acids, acetylcholine, and proteolytic enzymes.

Keep the source's qualification: it calls the ranking controversial and cites a textbook passage describing bradykinin as especially painful after tissue damage. The evidence supports bradykinin as a potent pain-producing mediator, but does not justify treating “most potent” as a universal ranking across every tissue, concentration, or experimental method.

Prostaglandin E2 commonly sensitizes nociceptors and can amplify bradykinin-evoked pain rather than acting as the source-keyed answer here. Substance P also participates in nociceptive transmission, so the source's grouping of it with sensitizing agents should not be read as a universal claim that it cannot excite nociceptive pathways.

rationales.a: Serotonin is an algogenic mediator, but the source's answer key selects bradykinin and explicitly cites it as the better answer.
rationales.c: Histamine can activate nociceptors, but it is not the source-keyed answer to this comparative item.
rationales.d: Prostaglandins are important pain sensitizers; the source distinguishes that role from the direct algogenic answer it keys as bradykinin.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The source explicitly labels the question controversial while using “most potent” as a broad comparative superlative. Relative algogenic potency depends on the experimental context, and the source explanation itself mixes direct algogens with sensitizers and neuropeptide signaling.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: The augmentation retains bradykinin as the exact source-keyed best answer, teaches it as a potent endogenous algogen, and avoids presenting an unsupported universal potency ranking. It also distinguishes PGE2 sensitization from bradykinin-evoked pain and preserves substance P's established nociceptive role.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q010.takeaway: TRPV1 responds to noxious heat, capsaicin and protons; vibration is not its defining activating stimulus, so vibration is the exception.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q010.displayText:
Vanilloid receptor 1 (TRPV1) is a nonselective cation channel expressed by nociceptive sensory neurons. It is activated by capsaicin and related vanilloids, noxious heat (classically around or above 43 °C), and protons/acidic conditions.

Vibration is not a defining TRPV1 stimulus; mechanosensation is primarily mediated by other transduction channels and receptor systems. Therefore vibration is the source-keyed exception. The source lists “Heat” and “Thermal” as separate choices even though they overlap, but this duplication does not change the keyed answer because both describe heat activation.

rationales.a: Noxious heat activates TRPV1, classically at temperatures around or above 43 °C.
rationales.b: Thermal stimulation is the same heat modality expressed in option A; it is not the exception asked for.
rationales.c: Chemical agonists such as capsaicin and protons activate or gate TRPV1.
